summary:
Visitors in Edo State stand under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. No source in this inventory applies Sharia criminal law to Edo State.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Edo State's own record is one of lethal community violence against men caught in same-sex acts, with no prosecution recorded in any of the incidents documented here. In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The Nigerian Observer's coverage framed the act as 'abominable' and as defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land'.

On 10 June 2010 the Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, Oredo Local Government Area, that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm, Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the mob then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. Lethal mob 'community justice' therefore operates in the state capital as well as in smaller communities, with no documented law-enforcement response.

Edo's police machinery has itself pursued same-sex couples on the ground. The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. A community lynching attempt was answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than by protection.

For national scale, The Initiative for Equal Rights' 2024 Human Rights Violations Report, published in January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics across Nigeria during the reporting period, and states that these figures represent only a fraction of the true scale.
tangentialFactors:
Edo State's documented incidents span 2008, 2010 and 2018, which indicates a persistent pattern of mob action against men caught in same-sex acts rather than an isolated event, and the direction of that pattern has not shifted across the period covered by these sources.

The two community incidents and the police response differ in kind: in Ekpoma and Benin City the mob acted first and no law-enforcement response is recorded, while in the 2008 case police arrived, arrested one partner and issued a wanted declaration against the other. In both variants the outcome for the men involved is exposure, flight or detention, not protection.

Edo's record sits inside a national picture in which the SSMPA supplies the legal basis for arrest and extortion, and community morality supplies the motive for killing. The two layers are documented independently: the national sources describe statute-based enforcement and app-based entrapment, while the Edo sources describe customary judgement operating lethally.

The TIERs national figures give a comparator for the Edo incidents: 556 violations affecting 850 victims in one year, described by the authors as a fraction of the true scale, against which three Edo incidents surfaced across seventeen years of press coverage.

Bobrisky's case is a Lagos and federal Correctional Service matter, not an Edo one, but it is the only sourced example of how a trans woman is placed within Nigerian custody, and placement was left to official discretion rather than decided by rule.
localsOnly:
Residents of Edo State face the same SSMPA exposure as everyone else in Nigeria, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and for cohabitation, public displays of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations. The twelve states applying Sharia criminal law are recorded as northern states; no source in this inventory applies that layer to Edo.

Police in Edo have used their powers against same-sex couples directly. The February 2008 incident in a remote community in the state ended with one partner arrested for interrogation and the other declared wanted over 'gay practice' by 15 August 2008, after a mob had already beaten both men.

Community enforcement is the more lethal layer for residents. The 2018 Ekpoma lynching and the 2010 Benin City mob attack both followed the discovery of men together in a private apartment or room, in each case after a neighbour or community member raised the alarm, and no prosecution of any attacker is recorded in the coverage of either.

Residents have no statutory protection to appeal to: Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The TIERs report published in January 2025 counts 556 violations affecting 850 victims nationally in 2024 and states that these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Trans residents are exposed through gender expression rather than through an explicit trans statute, and through custody practice: in Bobrisky's 2024 imprisonment the question of which section she was held in was openly debated in the press, and an October 2024 panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved by the sources in this inventory; no enactment date or statute is sourced here.

No prosecution, arrest or charge against any mob member is recorded in the reporting of the 2018 Ekpoma lynching or the 2010 Benin City attack, and whether any law-enforcement response followed either incident is not sourced. The absence is stated as unrecorded rather than as a finding of impunity.

Mark Osato Edomwonyi's whereabouts were still unknown when the Nigerian Observer filed its 10 June 2010 report; his subsequent fate is not sourced. The condition of Paddy, on whom the mob 'unleashed terror', is likewise not stated in the available material.

No Edo State-specific legislation, governor's directive, police command instruction or state protection mechanism for LGBTQ+ people is sourced in this inventory, and none is asserted.

Nothing in this inventory addresses document or gender-marker rules, entry and visa screening, access to gender-affirming care, or public facilities for visitors in Edo State; those questions remain not sourced rather than answered in the negative.

The TIERs figures cover Nigeria as a whole and are not broken down by state in the material available here, so the share of the 556 violations occurring in Edo State is unresolved.
